blocks.text: A robot arm swings a gripper on a rotating base while the gripper itself slides out along the arm. A camera on the arm sees only the sliding; a camera on the factory floor sees sliding plus sweeping. Telling those two viewpoints apart, and combining them, is what a rotating reference frame is for.

blocks.markdown: A reference frame $Oxy$ rotating with angular velocity $\omega$ (rad/s) carries unit vectors $\hat e_x$ and $\hat e_y$ that themselves change direction. The time derivative of a vector $\mathbf A$ seen by a fixed observer therefore has two parts: the rate at which $\mathbf A$ changes **as seen in the rotating frame**, plus the rate at which the frame turns it. This is the **transport relation**.

blocks.caption: Subscript 'rel' means the derivative seen by an observer rotating with the frame (components differentiated while $\hat e_x,\hat e_y$ are held fixed).

blocks.title: Absolute and relative velocity
blocks.text: The **absolute velocity** $\mathbf v_P$ is measured in the fixed frame. The **relative velocity** $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ is the velocity of $P$ as measured by an observer attached to the rotating frame. The frame's own velocity at the origin is $\mathbf v_O$. The two are related by the equation below.

blocks.caption: $\mathbf r$ is the position of $P$ from the origin O of the rotating frame (m). The term $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$ is the velocity of the point of the frame that is momentarily coincident with $P$.

blocks.markdown: For a slider on an arm that rotates about a fixed pivot ($\mathbf v_O=0$), use polar components: $\hat e_r$ along the arm and $\hat e_\theta$ perpendicular to it in the sense of positive rotation. A slider at distance $r$ moving along the arm at rate $\dot r$ has $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}=\dot r\,\hat e_r$ and $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r=r\omega\,\hat e_\theta$.

blocks.latex: \mathbf v_P=\dot r\,\hat e_r+r\omega\,\hat e_\theta,\qquad |\mathbf v_P|=\sqrt{\dot r^{2}+(r\omega)^{2}}
blocks.caption: The two components are perpendicular, so the speed follows from Pythagoras.

blocks.title: Slider on a rotating arm
blocks.prompt: An arm turns counterclockwise at 3 rad/s about a fixed pivot O. A slider is 0.5 m from O and moves outward along the arm at 0.8 m/s relative to the arm. Find its absolute velocity.

steps.text: Transverse component from the turning arm.

blocks.answer: $|\mathbf v|=1.70$ m/s, directed $61.9^\circ$ from the arm toward the sense of rotation.

blocks.title: Frame whose origin moves
blocks.prompt: A trolley moves at 2 m/s in the $+x$ direction. On it, an arm pivoted at O (on the trolley) turns counterclockwise at 4 rad/s. When the arm points along $+y$, a slider 0.3 m from O moves outward at 1.0 m/s relative to the arm. Find its absolute velocity.

steps.text: Rotation term: arm along $+y$ so $\hat e_\theta=-\hat i$ and $\omega r=4(0.3)=1.2$ m/s.

blocks.answer: $\mathbf v_P=(0.8,\,1.0)$ m/s with magnitude 1.28 m/s. The trolley and the turning arm partly cancel in the $x$ direction.

rows: 'speed relative to the ground' or 'as seen from the floor'
'sliding along the arm at...' or 'relative to the arm'
'the arm turns at...' or 'the trolley moves at...'
blocks.caption: Reading absolute and relative motion in problem statements.

blocks.title: Reading the problem
blocks.text: Decide first which observer each number belongs to. A speed 'along the arm' or 'relative to the arm' is $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$. A speed 'of the arm tip' or 'of the trolley' belongs to the frame. The speed 'of the slider' with no qualifier is normally absolute and must be found by adding everything.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Treating $\dot r$ as the absolute radial speed when $r$ changes while the arm turns (it is correct for the radial part but the transverse part $r\omega$ must be added), forgetting $\mathbf v_O$ when the pivot moves, and confusing the frame's rotation $\omega$ with the slider's angular rate.

points: The transport relation: fixed-frame derivative equals rotating-frame derivative plus $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf A$.

Absolute velocity of a point is $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_O+\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$; for a slider on an arm about a fixed pivot $\mathbf v=\dot r\hat e_r+r\omega\hat e_\theta$.
Read each quantity in a problem as absolute, relative or carrier motion before adding.

questions.stem: Which equation gives the absolute velocity of a point $P$ moving in a frame that rotates with angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega$ about an origin O moving with velocity $\mathbf v_O$?

distractorRationale.b: This holds only when the frame is not moving or rotating.
distractorRationale.c: The cross product is with the position vector, not the relative velocity.
distractorRationale.d: The terms add; they do not subtract.

questions.explanation: The absolute velocity is the sum of the velocity of the origin, the velocity of $P$ seen from the frame, and the velocity $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$ of the frame point coincident with $P$.

questions.stem: An arm turns at 5 rad/s about a fixed pivot. A slider is 0.40 m from the pivot and moves outward at 0.60 m/s relative to the arm. Find the speed of the slider in m/s.
questions.explanation: The radial component is $0.60$ m/s and the transverse component is $r\omega=0.40(5)=2.0$ m/s. The speed is $\sqrt{0.60^2+2.0^2}=2.09$ m/s.

questions.stem: An arm turns at 2.5 rad/s about a fixed pivot. A slider 0.80 m from the pivot moves inward along the arm at 1.5 m/s relative to the arm. Find the speed of the slider in m/s.
questions.explanation: The relative component has magnitude 1.5 m/s (directed inward) and the transverse component is $0.80(2.5)=2.0$ m/s. The speed is $\sqrt{1.5^2+2.0^2}=2.5$ m/s.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements gives a velocity measured relative to a rotating frame?

options.text: A bead slides along a spinning wire at 2 m/s as seen by an observer riding on the wire
A car travels at 20 m/s as shown by a roadside speed camera
A turntable has a rim speed of 3 m/s relative to the floor
A satellite orbits at 7.5 km/s as seen from a fixed inertial frame

questions.correctOptionText: A bead slides along a spinning wire at 2 m/s as seen by an observer riding on the wire

distractorRationale.b: This is measured in the ground frame, so it is absolute.
distractorRationale.c: This is the frame's own velocity at the rim as seen from the floor.
distractorRationale.d: This is absolute motion measured in an inertial frame.

questions.explanation: Relative velocity is what an observer fixed to the rotating or moving frame measures. The bead moving along the wire as seen by someone on the wire is the standard example.

questions.stem: A platform moves at 3 m/s in the $+x$ direction. On it, an arm pivoted at O turns clockwise at 2 rad/s. At the instant considered the arm points along $+x$, and a slider 0.5 m from O moves outward along the arm at 0.4 m/s relative to the arm. Find the absolute speed of the slider in m/s.
questions.explanation: The origin velocity is $(3,0)$ and $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}=(0.4,0)$. For clockwise rotation $\boldsymbol\omega=-2\hat k$, so $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r=-2\hat k\times0.5\hat i=(0,-1.0)$. Then $\mathbf v=(3.4,-1.0)$ m/s and $|\mathbf v|=3.54$ m/s.

questions.stem: A collar is clamped to a rotating arm at a fixed distance $r$ from the pivot. If the arm turns at $\omega$, what is the collar's absolute velocity (fixed pivot)?

options.text: Zero, because it does not move relative to the arm

distractorRationale.b: The velocity from rotation is always perpendicular to the radius.
distractorRationale.c: Relative velocity is zero but the frame itself moves the collar at $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$.

questions.explanation: With $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}=0$ and $\mathbf v_O=0$ only $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$ remains, with magnitude $r\omega$ and direction perpendicular to the arm.

questions.stem: A slider moves on an arm that turns about a fixed pivot. At the instant considered it is 0.50 m from the pivot, its speed relative to the arm is 2.4 m/s along the arm, and its absolute speed measured from the ground is 4.0 m/s. Find the angular velocity of the arm in rad/s.
questions.explanation: The radial relative component (2.4 m/s) and the transverse component $r\omega$ are perpendicular, so $r\omega=\sqrt{4.0^2-2.4^2}=3.2$ m/s. Therefore $\omega=3.2/0.50=6.4$ rad/s.

questions.stem: For which condition is the absolute velocity of a point equal to its velocity relative to a moving frame?

options.text: When the frame rotates at constant $\omega$ only
When the frame has zero origin velocity and zero angular velocity
When the point is at rest in the frame
Always, because velocity is a vector

questions.correctOptionText: When the frame has zero origin velocity and zero angular velocity

distractorRationale.a: The term $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$ is non-zero unless $\omega=0$ or the point is on the axis.
distractorRationale.c: Then $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}=0$ but the absolute velocity equals the carrier velocity.
distractorRationale.d: Velocity depends on the observer; frames in relative motion measure different velocities.

questions.explanation: With $\mathbf v_O=0$ and $\boldsymbol\omega=0$ the transport relation reduces to $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$. Otherwise the frame's motion adds a carrier velocity.

questions.stem: Derive the velocity transport relation $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_O+\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$ for a point $P$ in a frame rotating with angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega$ about an origin O.
markingGuide: Writes $\mathbf r_P=\mathbf r_O+\mathbf r$ with $\mathbf r=x\hat e_x+y\hat e_y$ in the rotating frame
Differentiates: $\mathbf v_P=\mathbf v_O+\dot x\hat e_x+\dot y\hat e_y+x\dot{\hat e}_x+y\dot{\hat e}_y$
Identifies $\dot x\hat e_x+\dot y\hat e_y=\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$
Uses $\dot{\hat e}_x=\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat e_x$ and similarly for $\hat e_y$, so the last terms equal $\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$
questions.explanation: The unit vectors of a rotating frame change direction at the rate $\boldsymbol\omega\times\hat e$, which produces the extra term. A fixed-frame observer sees both the change in $x,y$ and the turning of the axes.

questions.stem: A problem states: 'A tray on a lorry moves at 6 m/s relative to the road. A bead slides along a rotating spoke at 2 m/s relative to the spoke, which turns at 8 rad/s.' Identify, with reasons, which speeds are absolute, relative or carrier quantities, and explain what goes wrong if they are simply added as scalars.
markingGuide: Lorry speed 6 m/s relative to the road: velocity of the frame origin $\mathbf v_O$ (absolute, carried)
2 m/s along the spoke: relative velocity $\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}$ measured by someone on the spoke
8 rad/s: the angular velocity of the rotating frame; carrier velocity is $\omega r$, perpendicular to the spoke
Absolute velocity is the vector sum $\mathbf v_O+\mathbf v_{\text{rel}}+\boldsymbol\omega\times\mathbf r$
Scalar addition ignores directions: the components are generally perpendicular, so the magnitude is found from vector addition (e.g. Pythagoras for the spoke terms)
questions.explanation: The key skill is to tag each number with its observer before computing. The rotation contributes a velocity perpendicular to the spoke that depends on the distance of the bead from the pivot.
